Hacknet is a great intro to Unix command line interface.  There are lots of basic command line tutorials out there but to build muscle memory, you need to use commands like cd (change directory) and ls (list content) over a 100 times.  However who wants to change directory and list directory content over 100 times?  Thus most tutorials will let you practice a command couple times then move on--not building muscle memory.  Hacknet is the solution! In Hacknet you will connect to multiple computers on the net, traversing the file system via the command line and it before you know it you will build muscle memory.  The story is well written and compelling enough that typing the same commands over and over (grinding) to "flip the page" of the story is worth it.

If you are doing this for just the learning purposes--many realistic hacking game reviews recommend Hacknet as a prerequisite.  I recommend getting the Labyrinth expansion because it add new tools to learn.  When no new tools or commands are offered, start the Labyrinth expansion mission, The Kaguya Trials--start Labyrinth missions early rather than later.  Hacknet stops introducing new concepts about mid way and the Labyrinth expansion brings the learning back.   Mid Labyrinth missions, decide when you practiced enough and stop playing.

If I have to be honest, I'm pretty disappointed in this game.  The gameplay itself isn't particularly interesting and can get quite repetitive.  The world feels flat and uninteresting at times as many files that populate the directories of computers repeat themselves.  The story isn't all that interesting, and there's maybe one or two impactful choices in the entire game.
And yet, this game is far and away one of the best experiences I've ever had.  The game feels real in a way that no other game has before or since.  In most games, you play as either a character with their own emotions and desires, or a blank slate so you can insert yourself into the story.  In either case, the player and the protagonist are separate -- the protagonist exists in the world of the game, and you exist in the real world , and that's that.
Hacknet blurs those lines, though--you and the protagonist are one and the same. There's no character in game that represents you because you are them. By simply playing the game, you are breaking the fourth wall and bringing the game world with you to the other side.  The execution of this concept is done so perfectly that I frankly don't really care about the flaws this game has. I've never been so immersed in a game as I have been with Hacknet, and I don't think I ever will be again. This game does something that basically no other game has done, and for that I think its worth a buy.

[h1]Surprisingly good.[/h1]
If you have ever played Uplink, you have a fair idea of what is going on in the world of Hacknet: as an aspiring hacker, you enter the murky world, learn through contracts and eventually achieve your goals.

Featuring a well-written story, superbly appropriate soundtrack and a smooth and intuitive interface, Hacknet does well to draw you in and recreate the feeling of system reconnaissance with a view to breaching. While I feel the work is intended to be done mostly through CLI with the various commands provided, those of a less technical mind can still use the GUI for most functions (not all, actually hacking in requires the CLI and the various tools needed to gain access), removing that as a potential barrier to entry. The game also does very well in recreating an intense atmosphere, mostly through the ticking tracer: as the time ticks down it does place some stress on you as you try to breach, grab whatever information you came for, wipe your traces and disconnect again - before the clock hits 0.

The Labyrinths DLC is outstanding and virtually a mandatory purchase along with the base game. While in reality it is a standalone "campaign", it diverges radically from the base game with its mission structure, the interaction with contracts as well as the story. In general, DLC is a nice to have rather than a must have, but in this case Labyrinths is an almost integral part of the experience.

You will find it easier (although it is certainly not a requirement) if you have some Linux/Unix skills before starting. All can be done through the GUI provided, but the experience is best if you operate through the CLI - for which it is best to understand and be able to use commands such as ls, cat, rm, mv and so on. Its not a full implementation of Linux (e.g. you cannot remove filename.* from a directory - you either need to remove each individually or do rm *; autocomplete also does not work past the first level of directory structure) but it is close enough to immerse the player; it is a minor point anyway. I would also suggest either keeping a notepad open on another screen, or having pen and paper close to hand: it will make it easier to keep track of IPs, usernames/passwords, files and so on. Attention to detail is important and can often be the difference between a successful hack and an unsuccessful one.

Small rant: [spoiler]The devs did a great job of adhering to the octet numbering in the IP addresses (no octet can have a number higher than 255); why did they not respect the class system in the address space rather than using Class D/E on the "internet"?[/spoiler] Nitpicking, but for me it was slightly jarring.

It is a unique game and if the concept of a hacking "simulator" appeals to you, or if you have enjoyed Uplink in the past - do not miss out on Hacknet.

EXTREMELY buggy.

The game itself is quite nice but it is built on scenario triggers.

For example. You have a choosing from Missions 1 thru 5. But after you do 3 of those, you need to do a mandatory MISSION A which, after completing the goal, starts mandatory MISSION B in several seconds. Meanshile you get "emails" in your inbox which are akin to quest markers in your journal in other games.

So here's where the problems begin. 

MISSION A beings you on a QUESTLINE A.
MISSION B begins you on a QUESTLINE B,

If you opened email about mission B (or pressed "Reply", or ANYTHING), as soon as you complete MISSION B, QUESTLINE B is locked forever. You can still do QUESTLINE A, but Missions 4 and 5 are locked. 

OR

If you didn't manage to "Reply" to MISSION A, you are locked out of QUESTLINE A, and you don't have enough tools to complete QUESTLINE B either.

All of those questlines nevertheless lock you out of completing the MISSIONS 4 and 5 from the 5 I mentioned in the beginning. 

It's soooooo frustratingly designed and buggy, with arbitrary "oh don't press here, don't do this"... In a game that RELIES on you quickly pressing buttons and entering text... It's a freaking disaster.

What a shame.
